Six of Clubs playing card from a pack of transformation playing cards in which the various suit symbols e.g. hearts, spades, clubs, diamonds ('pips)' are overlaid on the image on the face of the card in such a way as to 'transform' or merge the pips into elements of the image. This lithograph printed card has a line drawing of a female figure in a floor length ornately embroidered period dress (circa late 18th century?) The dress has a low cut bodice going from shoulder to shoulder with crisscrossing stays tied in the front (like laces of sneakers) and a peplum flair at the waist. The effect is to both emphasize her bosom and minimize her waist. She has a pensive, demure demeaner however, and her dress has gauzy 'modesty' fabric from the top of her bosom that is gathered into a high neck where she wears a cross. Her sleeves are bell shaped and have a jaunty ribbon tied at the top of the visible shoulder. The bottom of hte dress is bell shaped as if she wore several crinolines. The fabric resembles brocade with a swirling leaf like pattern. She wears an apron-like cloth over the dress from her waist to about her knee. One dainty foot protrudes beyond the hemline. Her hair is obscured by a spade, but there is some hair ornament extending out what would be several inches on either side of her head. It resembles a stick with a ring at each end. She holds a watering can in her left hand (viewer right) apparently tending to her potted plants. Just below the watering can a leafy plant sits in a pot/vase that has an ogee type shape (like a stretched out 'S' on each side) on a pedestal base. On her right side (viewer left) she is tending a plant that resembles a flowering rose with several additional unopened blossoms. It rises from a pot that has an amphora shape with handles on each side shaped like a rectangular 'S' This pot sits on a base that looks a upside down scalloped cachepot (what you would normally put plants in!) At the top right there is a chandelier with four candles and a long downward protrusion from the middle made up of several bulbous shapes. The imagery is printed in brown ink on cream colored paper. The six spade shapes are solid black and appear as if they were block printed over the image. The are positioned as in typical playing cards: two at the top corners facing up, two in the middle facing down and two at the bottom corners facing down. The upper left spade is overlaid on the figure's hair suggesting a 'fascinator' hat. The upper right spade is overlaid on the center of the chandelier (as if it had some structural purpose to support the candles.) In the middle the left spade is overlaid on the central stem of the 'rose' plant (mimicing how the flowers spread from the center stem.) In the middle right, the spade faces is overlaid on the watering can, fititng within its borders as if it were a decoration on the can. At the bottom left, the spade is overlaid on the upturned cache pot as if it were a decorative element. And at the lower right the spade is overlaid on the vase fitting within its borders as if it were a decoration. The artist was very skillful in incorporating the spade symbols as design elements on this image. In this card, the complexity and delicacy of the details of the figure's dress, her lovely face, the flowers and pots, although rendered in monochrome brown, seem to balance the striking black shapes of the spades. While it is clearly a playing card, the figure does hold one's attention.
